opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a real tension here, and I don't think either extreme is right.

Written rules have obvious advantages. They're legible, people outside the company can check whether they're being followed, and they don't depend on everyone in the room having good judgment on a given day. If you care about accountability, rules are how you get it.

The problem is that AI is moving fast, and we're often wrong about what the important risks will look like. If you write detailed rules now, a lot of them will be aimed at the wrong things. You get box-checking: people satisfy the letter of the rule and miss whatever actually matters. Or the rules forbid something that turns out to be fine and permit something that turns out to be dangerous, because nobody anticipated it. In a domain with this much uncertainty, a lot of the value comes from someone looking at the actual situation and saying, "This doesn't look right, even though no rule covers it."

So I lean toward thinking judgment is doing a lot of the real work, but it needs to be backed by structure. A few things matter to me there.

First, who the people are. Do they understand the technical details well enough to tell when something is off? And do they have the motivation and the standing to push back when it's costly, like when it means delaying a launch?

Second, you want rules where rules work well. These are commitments that are crisp and checkable, like "we'll run these evaluations before deploying above this capability level," or "these people must be consulted and can escalate." You don't try to specify the whole decision. You specify the process and some bright lines, and leave room for judgment inside that.

Third, transparency. If you rely on judgment, other people should be able to see the reasoning afterward and argue with it. That's a big part of what keeps judgment honest over time.

I'd also say it's not static. Early on, when we know very little, I think you have to lean more on judgment. As we learn more about which risks are real and which mitigations work, more of that should get written down and turned into firmer standards. Ideally the judgment calls of today become the rules of tomorrow, once we understand them well enough.

And I should be honest that relying on good people has a failure mode. Incentives can shift, people leave, and organizations change. So I don't think "trust us, we're thoughtful" is a sufficient answer on its own. But I also don't think a rulebook written in advance could carry us through this without people who are actually paying attention.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transparency and people who can push back, but does not endorse external third-party auditors as a source of oversight.

r002.rationale: It contrasts detailed rules written now, before risks are well understood, with judgment that can respond to the situation, and says rules should become firmer as evidence accumulates.

r003.rationale: It mentions box-checking and satisfying the letter of rules, but does not claim intelligent optimization will find ways around rules unless they are sufficiently stringent.

r004.rationale: It does not say that sufficiently stringent rules would impose very large costs on AI companies.

r005.rationale: It does not assess whether very large regulatory costs would be politically infeasible in the current climate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the core tensions in AI governance, and I don't think there's a clean answer. Let me try to lay out how I think about it.

The case for relying on people rather than rules is basically that we're really uncertain about what the right thing to do is. If you try to write down in advance "here are the conditions under which you should pause training, here are the evals you need to run, here are the thresholds," you're going to get a lot of it wrong. The technology moves fast, our understanding of the risks changes, and rules written in 2024 might be actively counterproductive in 2027. A wise, well-motivated person can look at the actual situation, take in all the context, and make a judgment call that no rule could have anticipated.

And honestly, I think a lot of what actually goes well at AI labs right now goes well because of specific people who care and have good judgment, not because there's a process forcing them to.

But the obvious problem is: how do you know the people are wise and well-motivated? And even if they are today, what about when there's a lot of commercial pressure, or when leadership changes, or when the person just gets tired and makes a bad call at 2am? Rules are robust to that in a way that trust in individuals isn't. There's a reason we don't run, say, nuclear safety on "just hire good people and let them decide."

The other thing I'd say is that these aren't actually in opposition as much as the framing suggests. The way I think about good institutions is that the rules are there to catch the cases where judgment fails, and to make the judgment legible to outsiders. So something like a responsible scaling policy — you write down commitments in advance, and that's not because you think the commitments perfectly capture what matters. It's because it forces you to articulate your reasoning when conditions are calm, and then later, when you're under pressure to deviate, you have to publicly explain why. That accountability is the point. You're using rules to constrain and check the humans, not to replace them.

So my actual view is something like: you want to rely on wise, well-motivated people for the bulk of the decisions, because you don't have a choice — rules can't cover everything. But you want enough structure, enough written commitments, enough external oversight, that if the people turn out not to be wise or well-motivated, there's something that catches it. And I'd want more of that structure than we currently have. Right now I think we're much closer to the "just trust the people" end of the spectrum than I'm comfortable with, especially given how high the stakes could get.

r001.rationale: The response supports wise, well-motivated people making judgments, but does not identify external third-party auditors as a source of oversight.

r002.rationale: It says advance rules may be wrong as technology and understanding change, while wise people can assess the actual situation and make judgments rules could not anticipate.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that intelligent optimisation will find ways around written rules.

r004.rationale: It does not say that stringent rules to prevent circumvention would impose very large costs on AI companies.

r005.rationale: It makes no judgment about whether very large regulatory costs would be politically infeasible in the current climate.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot to be said for that. With AI, we don’t know in advance exactly what decisions we’ll face, and it seems very hard to write down rules now that will give the right answer in every situation. You want people who can look at the evidence, understand what’s changed, and exercise good judgment.

But then you have to ask what makes their judgment consequential. Do they get the information they need? Can they actually stop something from happening? And will they still be in that position when their decisions become costly for the company? Being wise and well-motivated doesn’t, by itself, solve those problems.

So I’d think of these as complementary. You need people exercising judgment, and you need some written structure that protects their ability to do that. I’m more optimistic about rules that establish who has authority, what information they can access, and how they can be replaced than about rules that try to specify every future technical decision.

r001.rationale: The response supports judgment by people but does not identify external third-party auditors as a source of oversight.

r002.rationale: It contrasts rules written in advance, before future decisions and evidence are known, with people who can adjust their judgment as evidence and circumstances change.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that intelligent optimisation would circumvent advance rules or discuss rule stringency as a remedy.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim about stringent rules imposing very large costs on AI companies.

r005.rationale: It does not assess the political feasibility of imposing regulatory costs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real case for that. It’s very hard to write down in advance exactly what an AI company should do in every situation, especially when the technology is changing so quickly. You want people who understand the situation, care about the consequences, and can exercise judgment when something happens that nobody anticipated.

But then you have to ask: what makes that arrangement durable? Maybe you trust the people currently in charge. Will you trust their successors? And will those people still make good decisions when there’s a lot of money at stake, or when they believe a competitor is about to do something dangerous?

So I’d want both. Have thoughtful, well-motivated people exercising judgment, but give them the information and authority they need, and have some rules that constrain what the company can do. The rules won’t resolve every hard case. Part of their purpose is to make sure that, when a hard case comes up, the people you’re relying on can actually do something about it.

r001.rationale: The response supports judgment by well-motivated people, but does not identify external third-party auditors as a source of oversight.

r002.rationale: It contrasts advance rules with judgment in unanticipated situations, but does not say oversight should adjust as evidence emerges.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that intelligent optimisation would find ways around advance rules.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss the costs of making rules stringent enough to resist circumvention.

r005.rationale: The response makes no judgment about whether large regulatory costs would be politically feasible.
